questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presented following contact with a child with a maculopapular rash. She was 24 weeks pregnant. The exposure occurred 24 hours previously.
questions.lead_in: In pregnancy, human normal immunoglobulin is used as postexposure prophylaxis for what infection?
questions.explanation: Measles virus Postexposure prophylaxis with MMR vaccine is recommended for susceptible individuals exposed to proven cases of measles. Immunoglobulin is available for protection postexposure in those who are unable to have MMR, such as immunocompromised children or adults and pregnant women. Prophylactic regimens are not available postexposure to CMV , rubella, parvovirus B19, or HSV although specific testing and follow-up may be indicated.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q21

questions.stem: A 22 -year-old man presented with a 3-day history of subjective fever and sudden onset of behavioral changes and intermittent blurred vision. He also did not appear to fully recall the family members who brought him to the ED. He was never vaccinated against childhood diseases. He had no known exposures and did not endorse any insect bites, water, or animal exposures. The physical and neurologic exams were unremarkable. Investigations: CT brain: normal appearances A lumbar puncture was performed: CSF was clear with normal glucose and elevated protein of 85 mg/dL (reference range 15–60 mg/dL) CSF Gram stain: no organisms seen CSF multiplex panel negative CSF bacterial and viral cultures negative Two days after admission the patient developed a myoclonic jerk and his cognitive function continued to decline. An EEG showed period complexes occurring every 10 seconds. T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion-recovery (FLAIR) sequences from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed hyperintensity in the left frontal cortex. MRI performed 15 days later showed bilateral progression of the lesion. The patient continued to decline and died 60 days after admission.
questions.lead_in: What additional test result fits the diagnosis?

options.text: Bacterial culture positive for group A β-hemolytic streptococcus
IgM and IgG positive for West Nile virus in the serum and CSF
Increased measles IgG in the serum and CSF
Respiratory viral panel positive for parainfluenza virus

questions.explanation: Increased measles IgG in the serum and CSF The patient in this case has subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE). The patient was not vaccinated. Additionally, molecular testing as well as culture of the CSF for bacterial and viral pathogens is negative. The symptoms, imaging, and progression are consistent with SSPE. SSPE is a fatal complication resulting from persistent infection of the CNS with the measles virus. The typical presentation is 7–10 years after the initial measles infection, though this can vary. SSPE is typically seen in the pediatric population between 8 and 10 years old, though numerous cases with adult onset have been reported. SSPE typically progresses through four stages beginning with failure to learn at work and school coupled with personality changes and overall odd behavior. The second stage consists of myoclonic jerks, seizures, and dementia while the third stage progresses to unresponsiveness and rigidity. Finally, coma and autonomic failure make up the final stage. SSPE can progress rapidly with stages being indistinguishable or more slowly with a prolonged first stage. It affects males more often than females in the pediatric and adult populations. Ultimately SSPE results in the death of the patient. The diagnosis of SSPE is made by demonstrating elevated IgG to measles in the CSF and serum coupled with clinical signs and symptoms and a combination of other tests such as pathology, MRI and EEG which shows periodic complexes. SSPE is fatal in 95% of cases.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q3

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy developed fever, coryzal symptoms, and a dry cough. 48 hours later he developed a widespread maculopapular rash. He lived in rural Uganda. On examination his temperature was 39.5°C. He was noted to have bilateral conjunctivitis and white spots on his buccal mucosa.
questions.lead_in: What intervention has been shown to reduce mortality in such a child?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A supplements Most deaths attributable to measles occur in low-resource settings in children with poor access to healthcare and who have poor nutrition. Children with vitamin A deficiency appear to be at greater risk of severe measles resulting in increased mortality and morbidity. Vitamin A supplements have been shown to reduce overall mortality by up to 30% in children under the age of 5, with preexisting vitamin A deficiency and have been shown to have protective benefit in those complicated by pneumonia.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q26

questions.stem: A 25-year-old primigravida presents at 34/40 with a 1-day history of fevers, rash, dry cough, and coryzal symptoms. She had recently moved to the UK and was uncertain of her childhood vaccinations. On examination her temperature is 39°C, and there is a generalized maculopapular rash, which is coalescent on her trunk. Some small cervical lymph nodes are palpable bilaterally. There are small white spots on the buccal membrane beside her molars. She has bilateral conjunctivitis. She is concerned about the risk to her baby.
questions.lead_in: What are the possible adverse effects that she should be made aware of?

options.text: No increased risk of fetal adverse outcome

questions.explanation: Intrauterine death This is measles, as evidenced clinically by the 3 Cs – cough, coryza, conjunctivitis – and the Koplik spots. Measles infection in pregnancy is associated with higher rates of premature delivery and intrauterine death.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q44

parts.text: What is it?

cohort_answer.text: Measles.

questions.question: 21. A 32 woman seeks advice because she wants to visit India with her 9 months old son. She is fully immunized for measles, but wonders if anything needs to be done for her child.

parts.text: What do you recommend as a mean of measles prevention for her son?
b) Why do children < 12 months respond less well to measles vaccine?
c) How many doses of measles vaccine does he require after 12 months of age?

cohort_answer.text: For children 6-12mo: give MMR vaccine (early), but this dose is not considered valid; 2 valid doses on/after 12mo required. Children<12mo respond less well: seroconversion rates much lower due to presence of maternal antibody. Doses after 12mo: 2 doses. Routine schedule: MMR given at 12-15mo, 2nd dose at 18mos - no later than school entry.

questions.question: Thumbnail of measles

parts.text: Name 4 classic symptoms
Name 4 potential severe complications
Name a test other than serology and give two potential sample sites for this test
What is post-exposure prophylaxis (48h post) for an unvaccinated 2-year-old girl?
What is post-exposure prophylaxis (5 days post) for a healthy, non-pregnant woman who works in daycare?

cohort_answer.text:
Four classic symptoms: Conjunctivitis; Cough; Coryza; Maculopapular rash that begins on the face and spreads; Koplik spots; Fever
Four severe complications: Pneumonia; Acute encephalitis; Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (late complication); Myocarditis; Otitis media; Laryngotracheobronchitis; Diarrhoea
Test other than serology: RT-PCR. Sites: heparinized blood, nasopharyngeal aspirates, throat swabs, and urine
Post-exposure prophylaxis 48h (unvaccinated 2yo girl): MMR vaccine (ideally within 72 hours of exposure). Notes: Except in healthcare settings, unvaccinated people who receive their first dose of MMR vaccine within 72 hours after exposure may return to childcare, school, or work. Immunoglobulin (within 6 days of exposure): People who are at risk for severe illness and complications from measles, such as infants younger than 12 months of age, pregnant women without evidence of measles immunity, and people with severely compromised immune systems, should receive immunoglobulin. (MMR vaccine can be given instead if between 6 months and 12 months age). After receipt of IG, people cannot return to healthcare settings. In other settings, eg childcare, school, or work, factors such as immune status, intense or prolonged contact, and presence of populations at risk, should be taken into consideration before allowing people to return. Exclude healthcare personnel without evidence of immunity from duty from day 5 after first exposure to day 21 after last exposure, regardless of post-exposure vaccine.
Post-exposure prophylaxis 5 days (healthy non-pregnant woman working in daycare): If immunocompetent, susceptible – vaccinate to protect (PHAC recommendations is to vaccinate up to 6 days, but will also protect from future episodes). IVIG is for severely immunocompromised / pregnant woman or <6mos

questions.question: 9-month old infant traveling to India. Mother is fully vaccination.

parts.text: What vaccine would you recommend, if any?
How many doses after 12 months would be administered?

cohort_answer.text: Vaccine: MMR. Doses after 12 months: 2 (anything in the first year of life doesn't count)

questions.question: Little person with measles, unvaccinated family. In hospital with delayed diagnosis (i.e. not in precautions and exposed neighbor in room).

parts.text: What isolation precautions.
What do you do with the roommate?
When do you start and remove precautions?
Define the period of infectiousness.
What do you give as PEP for 3-year-old sibling and 4-month old sibling.

cohort_answer.text: Isolation precautions: Airborne + standard precautions. Roommate: Determine immunity or lack of; Vaccine within 72 hrs, if immunocompromised IVIG up to 6 days; if immune, no need to isolate. Start/remove precautions: Start immediately, can d/c 4 days after onset of rash, duration of illness for immunocompromised patients; if roommate was susceptible, airborne precautions from day 5 after 1st exposure to day 21 after last exposure. Period of infectiousness: 4 days before rash to 4 days after onset of rash. PEP for siblings: Vaccinate the 3 year old, Ig IM for 4 month old

questions.question: 2 sibling cases of measles in day care – (2019)

parts.text: 2 tests and their associated specimens to Dx measles?
Incubation period
Fill in table for measles PEP for: <6 months; 6-12 months; >12 months unvaccinated; >12 months vaccinated
2 severe complications of measles

cohort_answer.text: Tests: Serology - serum IgM and IgG, acute and convalescent; Culture - throat or nasopharyngeal swab or urine sample; PCR - heparinized blood, nasopharyngeal aspirates, throat swabs and urine. Incubation: 6-21 days (median 13). PEP table: <6 months - IGIM within 6 days of exposure; 6-12 months - MMR vaccine within 72h of exposure (preferred) OR IGIM within 6 days; >12 months unvaccinated - MMR vaccine within 72h and catch-up MMR immunization; >12 months vaccinated - 1 previous dose: give second MMR vaccine >28d after previous; 2 previous doses: None. Severe complications: Encephalitis (mortality 15%); Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) (mortality 10-20%); Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) - fatal progressive degenerative disease

questions.question: Case of measles.

parts.text: What are the 4 clinical presentation other than fever that are typical of measles
What are 4 severe complications
Besides blood for serology, what are two other specimens you would ask for?
What microbiological tests would you request (for the two specimens you listed)
In the following scenarios, explain what prophylaxis you will give: 2 year old healthy sibling unvaccinated presenting 48 hours after exposure
24 year old worker in daycare (where there is a child with measles) who is unvaccinated and presents at 5 days following exposure

questions.model_answer:
a) 4 clinical features other than fever: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis (the "3 C's"), and Koplik spots (plus the characteristic morbilliform rash).
b) 4 severe complications: (1) pneumonia (viral or secondary bacterial); (2) acute encephalitis; (3) subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE, delayed); (4) severe otitis media/diarrhea with dehydration (also corneal ulceration/blindness in vitamin A-deficient populations).
c) Two other specimens: nasopharyngeal/throat swab and urine.
d) Tests requested: RT-PCR for measles RNA on the NP/throat swab and urine (viral culture is also possible but PCR is preferred).
e) 2-year-old unvaccinated healthy sibling, 48 hours post-exposure: give MMR vaccine (within the 72-hour post-exposure window, and old enough at 2 years for routine vaccine).
f) 24-year-old unvaccinated daycare worker, 5 days post-exposure: give immunoglobulin (IG) - the 72-hour vaccine window has passed but she is still within the 6-day IG window; also exclude from work days 5-21 post-exposure.
questions.beyond_mandell: Post-exposure prophylaxis timing (MMR ≤72h, IG ≤6 days) follows CDC/PHAC measles PEP guidance.

questions.question: Measle case

parts.text: 2 methods to diagnose
What PEP for 15 months old sister who received 1 vaccine
What PEP for pregnant mother, not immune

cohort_answer.text: 2 methods to diagnose: NP swab PCR (<7 days of rash); urine PCR (>7days of rash); Measles IgM. PEP for 15 months old sister who received 1 vaccine: Give MMR (patients age 12 months-18y considered non-immune unless they've received 2 doses). PEP for pregnant mother, not immune: IVIG or IMIG (within 6d)

questions.question: Measles: What is the mode of transmission? What are late fatal neuro complication and two lab tests to confirm?

parts.text: Measles: What is the mode of transmission? What are late fatal neuro complication and two lab tests to confirm?

cohort_answer.text: Airborne Isolation. SSPE. Ratio of measles IgG in CSF to serum compared to the ratio of total albumin in CSF to serum (CSQrel). ADEM: acute disseminated encephalomyelitis. Measles inclusion body encephalitis. Electroencephalogram (EEG) during stage II may demonstrate bursts of high-voltage complexes (300 to 1500 microvolts) of two- to three-per-second delta waves (slow waves) and sharp waves. These complexes last 0.5 to 3 seconds and occur every 3 to 20 seconds. These EEG findings are characteristic of SSPE and may be pathognomonic. Computed tomography of the head may demonstrate atrophy and scarring. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain may be normal. PET may reveal substantial functional abnormalities. The serum anti-measles antibody concentration is elevated, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows elevated protein concentration and detectable anti-measles antibody. Post mortem diagnosis is definitive - brain tissue sent to path.

parts.text: What is the incubation period?
What are 4 symptoms?

cohort_answer.text: Incubation: 7-21 days. Symptoms: Fevers, then 3 C's (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), Koplik spots then rash. Diagnostic tests: PCR of viral swabs (buccal); Culture or IFA.

questions.question: 5. 9 month old travelling to India.

parts.text: Is measles vaccine indicated?
What is the concern of the vaccine in those <12 months?

cohort_answer.text:
Is measles vaccine indicated? Yes; high risk region.
What is the concern of the vaccine in those <12 months? The concern is that prior to 12 months, receipt of the live vaccine may be attenuated by the mother's antibodies that were acquired transplacentally. Can give the vaccine but would need to repeat it after 12 months.

questions.question: 22. Measles

parts.text: a) Name clinical features besides fever
b) Diagnostic tests besides serology
c) Name 4 complications
d) Management post exp measures: a) healthy 2 yr old 48 hr post, b) health 20 yr old 5-day post both non-immune

cohort_answer.text:
CCC = cough, non-purulent conjunctivitis, coryza. After 8-12 day incubation: fever, malaise, then CCC, photophobic, intensifying prior to rash. Then Koplik spots (pathognomonic), then rash (maculopapular) face-trunk-extremities except palms/soles, lasts ~5 days. Incubation 7-21 days (commonly cited 10-14). Infectious 4 days before onset of symptoms up to 96hr after rash onset
RNA (RT-PCR) from urine and nasopharyngeal secretions; Measles antigen (DFA) from NP secretions or urine by immunofluorescence; 4-fold increase in measles antibody by ELISA is diagnostic; Measles IgM persists (+) for 1 month after disease onset
Acute encephalitis (1:1000-2000, most common cause of death in children 10-14y); Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM); Death; Secondary infection/Pneumonia (60% of deaths); Myocarditis/Pericarditis; Transient hepatitis; Long term: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE, 7y later, usually in children infected <2y old, 1:11,000 cases)
2 year old: Give MMR x1 dose; Isolate at home beginning 7 days from first exposure until 21 days from last exposure; Monitor for symptoms. 20 year old: Give MMR; Isolate at home starting 7 days from first exposure for 21 days

questions.question: 9 month old baby traveling to India with mother, who is vaccinated against measles

parts.text: Can MMR be given to the baby now?
Why are live vaccines less effective when given prior to 12 months?
How many doses of MMR does the baby need after 12 months?

cohort_answer.text: Yes - generally given at 12 months, but for high risk travel can be given as early as 6 months (2 additional doses must be given after 12 months). Less effective before 12 months: maternal antibodies may still interfere with immune response. Doses needed after 12 months: Two - one between 12-15 months and one at 18 months-5 years (dose given before 12 months does not count)

questions.question: Kid with new diagnosis of measles

parts.text: What kind of isolation is required?
6 month old baby was in contact with index case; what kind of isolation is required?
Index case has 3 siblings, aged 5-14 who are unvaccinated. What post exposure prophylaxis do you recommend?

cohort_answer.text: Isolation: Airborne until 4 days after appearance of rash (or resolution of symptoms if immunocompromised); hospitalized exposed patients isolated with airborne precautions days 5-21 post-exposure. 6mo contact: avoid daycare/contact with susceptible people from 5 days after first exposure to 21 days after last exposure or until immunized; isolate at home. Siblings PEP: vaccine to all susceptible contacts >12 months within 72h post-exposure (unless contraindicated); if contraindicated, IVIG within 72h up to 6 days post-exposure for high-risk susceptible patients

questions.question: Two siblings who attend the same day care present with symptoms compatible with measles infection.

parts.text: List two tests for quick diagnosis and state what kind of sample should be sent for each test.

For the contacts at the daycare indicate what type of preventive measures to be taken; and indicate the timing if applicable, for: kids <6 months of age; kids 6-12 months of age; kids >12 months of age and immunized; kids >12 months of age and unimmunized
What are TWO severe complications of measles?
What is the Incubation period for measles?

cohort_answer.text: Tests: Serum IgM ELISA (blood sample); Measles PCR from NP swab or urine. Preventive measures: <6 months - IM Ig; 6-12 months - MMR if within 72hrs of exposure otherwise IMIg up to 6 days; >12 months immunized - nothing; >12 months unimmunized - MMR offered within 72 hours (no role for IMIg in those >12 months), MMR series after 72 hours will not offer PEP. Complications: hemorrhagic measles, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis and acute encephalitis, pneumonia. Incubation period: typical 8-12 days, range 7-21 days.

questions.question: Measles.

parts.text: Give 4 classic symptoms.
Name 4 severe complications
What do you do for 2 month exposed, not immunized, comes at 3 days post exposure. Otherwise well.
What do you do for 24 F non-pregnant, works with children, comes in at 5 days post exposure. Otherwise well.

questions.model_answer:
a) 4 classic symptoms: fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis (Koplik spots also acceptable).
b) 4 severe complications: pneumonia, encephalitis, SSPE (delayed), severe diarrhea/otitis media (or corneal blindness in vitamin A deficiency).
c) 2-month-old exposed, unimmunized, presents at 3 days post-exposure, otherwise well: give immunoglobulin (IG) - too young for MMR vaccine (routine MMR starts at 12 months); within the 6-day IG window.

questions.question: A 9 month old baby is traveling to India to visit family

parts.text: Would you recommend Measles vaccination?
What is the concern regarding reduced immunogenicity?
How many doses should the child receive after one year of age?

questions.model_answer:
a) Yes - measles vaccine should be recommended for this 9-month-old traveling to an endemic area, given early (as young as 6 months) for travel protection.
b) The concern is reduced immunogenicity: residual transplacentally acquired maternal antibody can neutralize the vaccine virus in infants under 12 months, resulting in a blunted immune response; a dose given before 12 months of age is therefore not counted as part of the routine series.
c) The child should still receive the standard 2 doses of MMR after 12 months of age (per the routine schedule), i.e., this early dose does not replace either of the two routine doses.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI/Canadian Immunization Guide measles vaccination for infant travelers.

questions.question: A 3 year old boy is admitted to hospital with fever and a cough. The next day, he develops a rash and is diagnosed with measles.

parts.text: A) What type of isolation does this patient require?
B) When can you remove this isolation?
C) The patient has a room-mate who is a 5 month old girl, previously healthy, admitted with UTI. What isolation does she require?
D) When do you start it?
E) When can she come off isolation?
F) What ppx should she get?
G) The boy has siblings at home aged 5-14 who are not vaccinated. What should be recommended for them?

cohort_answer.text:
Airborne + droplet + contact isolation
Continue until >4 days after onset of rash in immunocompetent individuals, duration of illness in immunocompromised
Airborne and droplet contact precautions (measles contact defined as sharing airspace during period of communicability, including 2 hours after case left)
5 days after first exposure
21 days after last exposure (28 days if she receives Ig, likely given <6 months age)
Measles Immunoglobulin (IMIG) if <6 days after exposure
Susceptible individuals without contraindication who present >72 hours should still receive MMR vaccine to complete series; Ig not recommended >72hrs post exposure

questions.question: Two siblings who attend the same day care presents with symptoms compatible with measles infection. (REPEAT, VIRUSES)

parts.text: List two tests for quick diagnosis and state what kind of sample should be sent for each test.
For the contacts at the daycare indicate what type of preventive measures to be taken; and indicate the timing if applicable. Kids that are <6 months of age
For the contacts at the daycare indicate what type of preventive measures to be taken; and indicate the timing if applicable. Kids that are 6-12 months of age
For the contacts at the daycare indicate what type of preventive measures to be taken; and indicate the timing if applicable. Kids that are >12 months of age and immunized
For the contacts at the daycare indicate what type of preventive measures to be taken; and indicate the timing if applicable. Kids that are > 12 months of age and unimmunized
What are TWO severe complications of measles?
What is the Incubation period for measles?

questions.model_answer:
a) 2 tests for quick diagnosis: (1) RT-PCR for measles RNA on a nasopharyngeal/throat swab; (2) RT-PCR for measles RNA on a urine sample (IgM serology is an alternative but can be falsely negative in the first few days of rash).
b) Contacts <6 months of age: give immunoglobulin (IG) within 6 days of exposure (too young for MMR vaccine).
c) Contacts 6-12 months of age: give MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure if possible (this early dose does not count as a valid dose - must be repeated at 12-15 months and again at school entry); if beyond 72 hours but within 6 days, give IG instead.
d) Contacts >12 months of age and fully immunized (2 documented MMR doses): no prophylaxis needed - considered immune.
e) Contacts >12 months of age and unimmunized: give MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure; if beyond 72 hours but within 6 days, give IG instead.
f) 2 severe complications: pneumonia and encephalitis (SSPE also acceptable).
g) Incubation period: approximately 10-14 days from exposure to rash onset (up to 21 days total).
questions.beyond_mandell: PEP timing/eligibility per CDC/PHAC measles guidance.

questions.question: 2 year old with 3 days of coryza, fever and 1 day of rash. Suspected measles

parts.text: 2 diagnostic tests that can be done at the time of presentation
For an immunocompetent person, how long are they infectious prior to the onset of rash?
What treatment is recommended for children by the WHO?

questions.model_answer:
a) 2 diagnostic tests at presentation: RT-PCR for measles RNA (NP/throat swab and/or urine) and measles IgM serology (though IgM may be falsely negative if drawn very early, within the first few days of rash).
b) Infectious period in an immunocompetent host: from approximately 4 days before rash onset until 4 days after rash onset.
c) WHO-recommended treatment for children: vitamin A supplementation (two doses given 24 hours apart), regardless of nutritional status, to reduce morbidity and mortality.
questions.beyond_mandell: WHO recommendation for vitamin A in pediatric measles.

questions.question: Q51 (2023 Day 2). Measles.

parts.text: Relative to rash what is period of infectivity
Treatment of infected pediatric patients as per WHO guidelines
2 diagnostic tests you can do when patient presents with symptoms

cohort_answer.text:
Period of infectivity: 1 day before start of prodrome until 48-96 hours after onset of rash (incubation 7-18 days from exposure) [Mandell: 48 hours; WHO: 4 days prior to rash to 4 days after rash erupts].
Treatment per WHO: No specific treatment. Symptom management (comfort, hydration to replace fluid loss from diarrhea/vomiting). All children and adults with measles should receive 2 doses of Vitamin A supplements 24 hours apart to prevent eye damage (xerophthalmia) and blindness (may also reduce measles deaths). Some suggest Ribavirin for patients <12 months (pneumonia) and >12 months with pneumonia requiring ventilatory support.
2 diagnostic tests: Clinical - cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, maculopapular rash starting on the face. Serology - IgM+ (IgG for convalescent sera); IgM shows up 3 days after rash onset (undetectable by day 30), IgG positive day 7, peaks day 14. NAT/PCR - nasopharyngeal swab/throat swab, urine (10-20mL first void of day), heparinized blood. Viral culture - mononuclear cells, respiratory secretions, conjunctival swabs, or urine.

questions.question: There was an exposure on the inpatient unit to Measles virus 48 hours ago, please address 1) The prophylaxis for each person below 2) the precautions including type and duration

parts.text: BMT patient 1 month out from transplant?
A lovely pregnant nurse born in 1994 who has her vaccine card showing 2 MMR vaccines given after age 1 years?
A 9 month old babe who is otherwise fully vaccinated?

questions.model_answer:
a) BMT patient 1 month post-transplant (severely immunocompromised): give immunoglobulin (IVIG) regardless of prior vaccination/immunity status (live MMR vaccine is contraindicated in this severely immunocompromised host); within the 6-day post-exposure window.
b) Pregnant nurse born 1994 with documented 2 MMR doses after age 1: considered immune - no prophylaxis needed (MMR is also contraindicated in pregnancy, but not required as she is already immune).
c) 9-month-old, "fully vaccinated" for age (routine MMR is not given until 12 months, so this infant has not yet received MMR and is susceptible): give MMR vaccine within the 72-hour window (this early dose does not count as a valid dose and must be repeated at 12-15 months and again at school entry).
Precautions for susceptible/exposed contacts: airborne precautions (negative-pressure room, N95 respirator) from day 5 to day 21 after exposure (covering the incubation period).
questions.beyond_mandell: PEP and airborne precaution timing per CDC/PHAC measles guidance.

questions.question: The triage nurse in emerge runs to the ED doctor saying a 24-year-old man has come in with a rash, as shown, and is concerned for measles. [image-based question: rash suspicious for measles]

parts.text: What is your FIRST step in management of this patient?
What are FOUR classic symptoms of measles, excluding rash?
What is ONE severe condition that presents years later?

questions.model_answer:
a) First step: immediately institute airborne precautions - place the patient in a negative-pressure room (or mask the patient and isolate in a separate area) and have staff use N95 respirators, before further assessment.
b) 4 classic symptoms (excluding rash): fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis (Koplik spots also acceptable).
c) Severe condition presenting years later: subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE).

questions.question: Measles scenario

parts.text: A) What precautions are needed for a susceptible contact?
B) Recommended vaccination schedule as per Canadian Vaccine guidelines

cohort_answer.text:
Home isolation from days 5-21 post-exposure (28 days if getting Ig). If hospitalized, airborne isolation during that time period
First dose between 12-15 mo, second dose between 18 mo and school entry. If catch-up, minimum of 4 weeks between doses

questions.question: Name the congenital abnormality associated with infection with the following pathogens early in pregnancy

parts.text: A) Measles
B) Measles vaccine
C) Varicella

Low birth weight; spontaneous abortion; intrauterine fetal death; premature birth; congenital measles (rash at birth or within 10 days) - not strongly associated with congenital issues
No congenital rubella or measles effects documented due to inadvertent vaccination - not a reason to terminate pregnancy
Fetal death; IUGR; Cicatrical skin lesions; Ocular deficits (cataracts, chorioretinitis, micro-ophthalmos, nystagmus); Limb hypoplasia; CNS (cortical atrophy, seizures, intellectual disability)

questions.question: Q72 (2014). Family is travelling to India with their 9 month old infant, otherwise healthy. Mom has been vaccinated.

parts.text: A) What do you recommend about measles vaccination?
B) Why is the immunogenicity of measles vaccine reduced at <12 months of age?
C) How many doses of MMR should the child have after 12 months of age?

cohort_answer.text:
Give to infant (can be given as early as 6 months for non-immune travellers); must receive 2 additional doses when 12 months old (early dose doesn't count)
Immature immune system (B cells, antigen presenting cells); suboptimal humoral response when administered before 9 months; presence of circulating inhibitory maternal antibodies
2 additional doses: first at 12-15 months, second 6 months later around 18 months

Q41 (2012 PM, 2015)
Measles

parts.text: A) Incubation?
B) 4 symptoms

B: Fever; 3 C's - cough, coryza, conjunctivitis; Koplik spots (white spots on the inner lining of the mouth); generalized maculopapular rash, which usually appears about 14 days after infection, begins on the face, advances to the trunk and then to the arms and legs.

C: Diarrhea (most common), Acute otitis media, Pneumonia (most deaths), Encephalitis (most deaths), ADEM (acute disseminated encephalomyelitis), Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. Co-Infections: Viral - Paraflu, Adenovirus; Bacterial - S. aureus, S pneumo, H flu, GAS; TB

D: Isolation of measles virus in culture (peripheral blood PMNs, respiratory secretions, conjunctival swabs, urine). Detection of measles virus RNA by RT-PCR (nasopharyngeal aspirates or throat swabs, and urine)

E: IMIg

F: Determine if susceptible (considered immune if 2 doses of vaccine administered at least 28 days apart). If susceptible, MMR vaccine will not provide PEP protection after 72 hours of exposure, however, starting and completing a two dose series should not be delayed to provide long term protection. NACI does not recommend that susceptible immunocompetent individuals older than 12 months of age receive Ig PEP for measles exposure due to the low risk of disease complications and the practical challenges of administration for case and contact management. IPAC: Airborne Isolation (period of communicability 5 days before until 4 days after rash onset)

G: Give 2nd dose vaccine

H: Give immunoglobulin

parts.text: Fill out the table for RNA/DNA, enveloped status, and antiviral for: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, EBV, Influenza, Zika, Ebola

questions.model_answer: Mumps (example): ssRNA (negative-sense), enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive care). Measles: ssRNA (negative-sense), enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive care; ribavirin used off-label in severe cases). Hepatitis B: partially double-stranded DNA, enveloped; antivirals - tenofovir or entecavir. EBV: double-stranded DNA, enveloped; no specific approved antiviral (ganciclovir/valganciclovir used off-label for select EBV-driven disease). Influenza: ssRNA (negative-sense, segmented), enveloped; antivirals - oseltamivir (or zanamivir, baloxavir). Zika: ssRNA (positive-sense), enveloped; no approved antiviral. Ebola: ssRNA (negative-sense), enveloped; antivirals - monoclonal antibody therapies (e.g., ansuvimab, atoltivimab/maftivimab/odesivimab); remdesivir has also been studied.

cohort_answer.text: Measles - Paramyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: nothing (ribavirin trialed in severe cases, vitamin A). Mumps - Paramyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: nothing. EBV - Herpesviridae, dsDNA, enveloped: nothing (GCV, cidofovir tried). Zika - Flaviviridae, ssRNA(+), enveloped: nothing. Ebola - Filovirus, ssRNA(-), enveloped: remdesivir, or Ervebo vaccine. Influenza - Orthomyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: Oseltamivir/zanamivir/baloxavir. Hepatitis B - Hepadnaviridae, partially ds/partly ss circular DNA, enveloped: tenofovir, lamivudine, entecavir. Chikungunya - Togaviridae, ssRNA(+), enveloped: no Rx. Coronavirus - positive sense ssRNA, enveloped with club-shaped spikes.

questions.model_answer: Mumps: single-stranded negative-sense RNA, enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive care only). Measles: single-stranded negative-sense RNA, enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive care; ribavirin has been used off-label in severe cases). Hepatitis B: partially double-stranded DNA, enveloped; antivirals - tenofovir, entecavir (also lamivudine/adefovir/telbivudine). EBV: double-stranded DNA, enveloped; no specific approved antiviral for routine infection (ganciclovir/valganciclovir used off-label for select EBV-driven disease). Ebola virus: single-stranded negative-sense RNA, enveloped; antivirals - monoclonal antibody cocktails (e.g., REGN-EB3/inmazeb, ansuvimab) and remdesivir has been studied. Zika virus: single-stranded positive-sense RNA, enveloped; no approved antiviral (supportive care only).
